articles.exam: A2 Key · Reading Part 2 (true / false / doesn't say)
articles.headline: Jonathan, the 194-year-old tortoise
articles.standfirst: Scientists have studied the DNA of the oldest land animal in the world.
body: Jonathan is a giant tortoise. He lives on Saint Helena, a small island in the South Atlantic Ocean. Scientists believe he is 194 years old, so he is the oldest land animal in the world. He came to the island in 1882.

Now scientists have studied Jonathan's DNA. DNA is the code inside every living thing. It tells the body how to grow and work. The team found special patterns on some of his genes. These genes help the tiny parts inside his cells that make energy. The patterns look like the ones in much younger tortoises.

Scientists do not know yet if this is the reason for his long life, so they want to do more tests. Jonathan lives in the garden of Plantation House, the home of the island's governor. In 2009 he was blind and not well, but a vet fed him by hand, and soon he was stronger.

glossary.d: the code inside a living thing that tells its body how to grow
small parts of DNA that carry information about the body
the very small parts that make up every living thing
the person who leads an island or a region for a country
not able to see

articles.headline: A shark in the city: crowds watch Bukangi
articles.standfirst: A big shark has swum into a canal in Busan, and people want to help her go home.
body: In Busan, a big city in the south-east of South Korea, there is a shark in a canal. A canal is a narrow channel of water made by people. The shark is female and about three metres long. People call her Bukangi. Someone first saw her in the canal last month.

Experts want to help Bukangi return to the open sea. They have tried three times to guide her with nets. Many people go to the canal every day to watch. There are very big crowds, and they hope the shark will be safe.
Why is she there? Experts think the water in the canal was unusually warm and full of fish. Perhaps the shark came to find food. Now she needs to find the way back to the sea.

articles.headline: How many visitors is too many? A new study for Machu Picchu
articles.standfirst: Peru will measure how many tourists the famous Inca site can welcome without being damaged.
body: Machu Picchu is one of the most famous places in Peru. Every year, thousands of visitors travel to the old Inca city in the mountains of Cusco. Now the government wants to know how many people the site can receive in a safe way.

Rogers Valencia, the Minister of Foreign Trade and Tourism, announced that experts will carry out an updated study called "Carrying Capacity and Limit of Acceptable Change". In simple words, it should help the authorities decide how many visitors the sanctuary can welcome without harming it.

The minister explained that the research will give a scientific base for decisions about visitor flow, the protection of the heritage and the quality of tourist services. He spoke at a meeting of the Machu Picchu Management Unit, a group that brings together several ministries and local authorities. It is led by the governor of the Cusco region, Werner Salcedo.

At the meeting, the group also looked at the situation of the Hiram Bingham Highway, the main road between the town of Machu Picchu and the citadel. The Minister of Culture and the Minister of the Environment also took part. The ministers said they will keep working together to protect the sanctuary for the future.

articles.headline: Who was in the Roman coffin? A mystery at Westminster Abbey
articles.standfirst: An archaeologist thinks he knows who lay inside a stone coffin found in London almost 200 years ago.
body: A Roman stone coffin has been a mystery at Westminster Abbey in London for a long time. The coffin, called a sarcophagus, was found in 1820 and officially dug up in 1869 from the grass next to the abbey's main hall. Inside there was a skeleton, but nobody knew who the man was, and people thought the skeleton had been lost.

The sarcophagus is from the fourth century and has a Latin name on it: Valerius Amandinus. But archaeologist Warwick Rodwell says the coffin was not first buried at the abbey. Later, a large cross was carved on its lid. In 2018, experts took the coffin to a laboratory, opened the lid and found the skeleton inside.

Tests showed that the bones belonged to a man between 35 and 49 years old, about 5 feet 9 inches tall. Radiocarbon dating gave a date from the late tenth or early eleventh century. Rodwell now believes the man was an abbot, the leader of a group of monks. "Nobody of lower rank would have been buried in anything like that," he said.

He thinks the best candidate is Ælfwig, who died around 1020 and led the abbey for about 27 years. Another possibility is Wulfnoth, who died around 1049. Rodwell says that archaeology is often more complicated than it first seems.

glossary.d: a stone coffin, often with carvings
all the bones of a body
a room where scientists do tests
the leader of a group of monks in an abbey
a person who could be the right answer

articles.headline: "It is certain that it will rain": Peru prepares for a stormy summer
articles.standfirst: Forecasters warn that El Niño could bring up to 300 millimetres of rain in a single day to the north coast in 2027.
body: Peruvians living on the northern coast may see extreme rainfall next summer. According to a spokesperson for the national weather service, Senamhi, totals of up to 300 millimetres could fall in a single day in the first months of 2027. To picture this, remember that one millimetre of rain equals one litre of water on every square metre of ground.

The warning follows the latest bulletin from ENFEN, the multisectoral commission that studies El Niño. It describes the 2026–2027 Coastal El Niño as an "extraordinary" event that will continue until January, before turning "strong" and lasting into the autumn. Sea-surface temperatures are expected to stay high, and new Kelvin waves, which carry warm water, may help to prolong the phenomenon. In other words, the ocean is likely to remain warm for months, which is one of the main conditions for heavy rain on the Peruvian coast.

Yet the Senamhi meteorologist, Nelson Quispe, was careful not to promise too much. The intensity of the rain, he explained, depends not only on the ocean but also on how the atmosphere responds, so nobody can yet say exactly how far the rainfall will exceed normal levels. Projections will have to be updated as conditions change. "It is certain that it will rain," he said, but the amount remains uncertain.

The first significant downpours are expected in November, in specific areas and with dry spells in between. After that, precipitation should increase progressively, becoming more frequent and more intense as the summer of 2027 arrives. There are already signs of change: in September, some places in Tumbes received up to 70 millimetres, far more than is typical for that month. Meanwhile, parts of the southern highlands and other regions could face a shortage of rain, which might affect farming and the refilling of reservoirs.

articles.instructions: For each question, choose the paragraph (A–F). Each paragraph can be chosen once.
articles.headline: Peru's exports are racing ahead of its neighbours
articles.standfirst: A UN regional report expects Peru to post the fastest export growth in Latin America and the Caribbean this year.
body: A. Peru is on course to record the highest export growth in Latin America and the Caribbean in 2026. The Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, known by its Spanish initials CEPAL, forecasts an annual increase of 30 per cent, helped by the high prices of metals such as copper and gold.

B. The gap with other countries is wide. Mexico is expected to grow by 26 per cent, while the regional average is 20 per cent. Argentina follows with 19 per cent, Ecuador and Brazil with 16, Colombia with 15 and Chile with 13.

C. In figures, Peru's exports were worth about 76.4 billion dollars in 2024 and nearly 94 billion in 2025. This year they could reach 122.4 billion. Services are growing more slowly, rising from 7.6 billion dollars to 8.5 billion.

D. Peru is also forecast to enjoy the biggest improvement in its terms of trade, a measure that compares the prices a country receives for what it sells with the prices it pays for what it buys. The growth is put at 25 per cent, against 11 per cent for Chile and Colombia and just 1 per cent for Mexico.

E. The report places these results in a changing world. Supply chains are being reorganised, demand for critical minerals is rising and major powers are using trade and technology as tools of strategic competition. At the same time, the region gains from the value of resources linked to the energy transition, food security and clean energy.

F. Even so, CEPAL warns that the challenge is not simply to sell more raw materials. The goal, it argues, is to use these resources to build activities with higher added value, including modern services that can be exported.

the network of companies and steps that make and deliver a product
the extra worth created when raw materials are turned into finished goods or services

articles.headline: From pond to brain: the tiny alga behind a Nobel prize
articles.standfirst: A one-celled organism that swims towards light has given scientists a tool to study the mind.
body: Some of the most powerful ideas in medicine begin in unlikely places. This month's Nobel prize for physiology or medicine, awarded to three scientists, rests partly on research into Chlamydomonas, a one-celled alga that most of us would never notice.

The organism swims towards light, and it does so with the help of a light-sensing protein called channelrhodopsin, which is strikingly similar to the rhodopsin found in the human eye. When the protein detects light, electrically charged particles called ions rush into the cell from outside. That triggers an electrical signal, astonishingly fast, which tells the alga to move its hair-like motor.

The researchers' insight was to borrow this natural switch. They transferred the alga's gene for channelrhodopsin into living animal brain cells, so that flashes of light could turn individual neurons on or off. The approach, often called optogenetics, has allowed scientists to pinpoint the exact circuits in the brain that control behaviour, feelings, memories, movement, sleeping and waking. It has even revealed how a mouse gathers its young in a nest or grooms them.

Why does this matter? The brain is hard to study because simply watching it shows what happens, not what causes what. Being able to switch a chosen group of neurons on or off with a flash of light lets researchers test cause and effect directly: if lighting up a circuit changes a behaviour, that circuit must play a part in it. The method turns a passive observation into a genuine experiment.

The applications reach well beyond the laboratory curiosity. The technique is being used to investigate depression, anxiety and Parkinson's disease, and it is being tested as a way of partially restoring vision in people with diseases of the retina.

The story offers a quiet lesson about how science works. Nobody could have predicted, when researchers first studied how a pond alga finds light, that the work would one day shed light on the human brain. Curiosity-driven research, which can look like an esoteric luxury, sometimes turns out to be the most valuable investment of all.

articles.headline: One bad apple? How other people's rule-breaking can spread
articles.standfirst: An experiment suggests that seeing others go further than the rules allow can make us bend them too.
body: Leaders caught in scandal often describe the culprit as a "bad apple", an isolated individual whose behaviour says nothing about the barrel. New research, however, lends support to the older version of the proverb: one bad apple can indeed spoil the rest. Molleman points out that many people, especially in individualist cultures such as the Netherlands and the UK, imagine themselves making autonomous decisions, when in fact they are very much influenced by what others do.

Dr Lucas Molleman, of the University of Amsterdam, and his colleagues wanted to understand how people decide whether to break rules when others are watching. They recruited 750 participants in the United States for an online task. Each had to pick the square, among 100, that glowed most brightly as an animated shooting star passed, and the correct choice earned a reward. But squares further to the right paid more, so cheating was profitable. Participants then saw whether another player had followed the rules, how far they had strayed and what their political leanings were, and could change their answer. The process was repeated six times.

Even at the start, 23 per cent of choices went for the most lucrative square. Seeing rule-followers modestly reduced cheating, and small, convenient violations nudged it up slightly. The decisive effect came when people witnessed flagrant breaches: they then raised their own rule-breaking sharply, sometimes exceeding what they had seen. The effect was stronger when the other player shared the participant's political outlook. Computer simulations suggested that a minority of escalating individuals could push a whole group out of control.

Yet the picture is not entirely bleak. About a third of participants obeyed the rules throughout, even though that cost them money. And Prof Stephen Reicher, of the University of St Andrews, who was not involved, urged caution. The task was abstract and carried no penalty, so the real-world relevance remains unproven. More importantly, he argued, the results do not support a simple theory of contagion: whether we are influenced depends on who the others are. We do not riot just because others do, he said, and many people who witness rioting help to clean up afterwards.
